source: McCarthy (1980; 1986 reprint) Circumscription: a form of non-monotonic reasoning
finding: Names the qualification problem: rules like 'a boat crosses a river' have endless unstated exceptions (leaky boat, missing oars, bridge, helicopter). Circumscription is a rule of conjecture: assume the only objects with a property are those the known facts force to have it. Conclusions are withdrawn when new facts are added.
numbers: Worked example: Missionaries and Cannibals, state (331) to (000), 11-step solution in Amarel's representation. A bridge is excluded until the problem statement mentions one.
quote: Circumscription is a rule of conjecture that can be used by a person or program for "jumping to certain conclusions".
limits: The conclusion is only as good as the claim that all relevant facts were taken into account. Pure logic, no human or machine data.
agent_relevance: Defaults stand for an open-ended list of exceptions we cannot enumerate. This is the formal reason to hold a conclusion until a concrete blocker appears (G1), not to hunt for blockers on a schedule.

source: McCarthy (1980) Circumscription, formal definition and minimal entailment
finding: Predicate circumscription is a second-order schema added to a first-order theory A: P holds only of what A forces. Semantics: A minimally entails q if q is true in every model of A that is minimal in P. Theorem: every instance of the circumscription schema is true in all minimal models (soundness). Several predicates can be circumscribed jointly.
numbers: Blocks example: from isblock A, B, C circumscription gives 'only A, B, C are blocks'. The paper says circumscription is not itself a nonmonotonic logic but nonmonotonic reasoning added to first-order logic.
limits: Minimal models do not always exist (Davis 1980, cited by McCarthy). Needs second-order or schema instances, so no general proof procedure. The choice of predicate to minimise matters.
agent_relevance: A retract-on-conflict rule can be coded as: keep a set of abnormal flags minimised unless a fact forces them. Code can do this over a small closed vocabulary, not over free text.

source: McCarthy (1980) Circumscription, addendum on Reiter and McDermott-Doyle
finding: Circumscription differs from McDermott-Doyle and Reiter in two ways: it concerns minimal models while theirs concern arbitrary models; and it is a schema in the base language while theirs add new inference rules or operators. The addendum gives a train-and-tracks example that is a non-normal default: 'if a train may be present, it is unsafe to cross', which concludes danger on mere possibility.
numbers: The example needs the possibility operator M; McCarthy replaces it with a schema or second-order formula.
limits: Dated text with a 1986 addendum; informal.
agent_relevance: Some defaults are safety defaults (conclude danger on possibility), not belief defaults. Our Revise rule should know which direction a default is allowed to jump.

source: McCarthy (1986) Applications of circumscription to formalizing common sense knowledge
finding: Lists uses of non-monotonic reasoning, including a communication convention (if a bird cannot fly and it matters, the speaker must say so) and a streamlined stand-in for probability when numbers are unavailable. Introduces the ab (abnormal) predicate with aspects: ab(aspect1 x) for one respect only, so a bird abnormal for flying is not abnormal in every respect. Axioms: birds fly unless ab(aspect2); ostriches and penguins cancel inheritance; species are disjoint.
numbers: Example set: bird, ostrich, penguin, canary; Tweety (canary) flies, Joe (ostrich) does not. Circumscribe ab with ab, flies, bird, ostrich, penguin as variable. Without the cancellation axioms only a disjunction is derivable.
quote: Clearly the program will have to include domain dependent heuristics for deciding what circumscriptions to make and when to take them back.
limits: Wrong choice of what to vary gives only disjunctions. Unique-names hypothesis not handled well; author says he does not know a completely satisfactory way.
agent_relevance: Aspect-indexed abnormality is a clean model of lessons with narrow scope: a failed lesson marks abnormality in one respect only, not the whole rule. Fits lesson memory with exceptions per aspect.

source: McCarthy (1986) Applications of circumscription: Reiter's two examples (Nixon; wife and employer)
finding: Nixon diamond: Quakers are normally pacifists, Republicans normally not. Systems that infer negation from non-provability give a contradiction. Circumscribing ab gives only 'Nixon is abnormal in aspect1 or aspect2', so there is no pacifism verdict and no contradiction. Second example: a person normally lives where his wife lives and where his employer is; wife in Vancouver, employer in Toronto.
numbers: Two conflicting defaults, one individual in both classes.
limits: The result is a disjunction, i.e. suspended judgment. There is no way to prefer one default without extra priority.
agent_relevance: When two defaults conflict and nothing ranks them, the logical output is 'undetermined', not a pick. G6 still requires a best guess at the end, so the pick must come from code-run checks, not from the logic.

source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (Strasser and Antonelli) Non-monotonic Logic: Reiter's default logic
finding: Reiter (1980): a default theory is a pair (Gamma facts, Delta defaults). A default (gamma : theta)/tau means: if gamma is known and theta is consistent with what is believed, conclude tau. An extension is a fixed point: Xi_0 = Gamma; Xi_i+1 = Cn(Xi_i) plus tau for each default whose prerequisite is in Xi_i and whose justification's negation is not in the final Xi. The definition is circular on purpose: consistency is checked against the final set.
numbers: No data. Formal definition as given by the review. Extension existence is not guaranteed in general; normal default theories always have one.
quote: Essentially, one has to "guess" a set of sentences, and then verify that it satisfies the definition of an extension.
limits: Secondary source on Reiter 1980; the original paper sits behind a publisher wall and was not opened. Consistency checks are not computable in general (non-semidecidable).
agent_relevance: Reiter's justification slot is the machine form of 'doubt only on a signal': a default fires unless its stated justification is contradicted. In code the signal is a failed check that adds the negation of the justification.

source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Non-monotonic Logic, Nixon diamond and skeptical versus credulous reasoning
finding: The Nixon diamond gives two extensions (pacifist; not pacifist). A credulous reasoner accepts conclusions of any extension; a skeptical reasoner accepts only what holds in all, so refrains from both. Floating conclusions (extended diamond: both branches imply 'Nixon is political') split the theories: some skeptical systems drop it, others keep it.
numbers: Qualitative. Competing consequence notions: skeptical, credulous, argumentation-based (Dung style).
limits: Which is right is a design choice with no empirical resolution in the review.
agent_relevance: When two attempts disagree and nothing ranks them, a skeptical stance means no commit from that pair. G6 forbids abstaining on the first pass, so use a credulous pick checked by code.

source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Non-monotonic Logic, KLM preferential consequence
finding: Kraus, Lehmann, Magidor (1990): defeasible consequence |~ is characterised by Reflexivity, Left Logical Equivalence, Right Weakening, Cut, Cautious Monotony and OR. These are the conservative core and correspond to preferential models (models ordered by normality, keep the minimal ones). Gabbay (1985) had argued earlier that Reflexivity, Cut and Cautious Monotony are the basic principles.
numbers: Cut: if phi&psi |~ tau and phi |~ psi then phi |~ tau. Cautious Monotony: if phi |~ psi and phi |~ tau then phi&psi |~ tau.
limits: Rational Monotony is more contested: Stalnaker (1994) gave a counterexample. Preferential semantics assumes one normality order.
agent_relevance: Cautious Monotony is the formal safety rule for memory: adding a conclusion the agent already holds must not erase other conclusions. A lesson-store update can be tested against it in code.

source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Non-monotonic Logic, rational closure and lexicographic closure
finding: Lehmann and Magidor (1992) rational closure: give each formula a rank (how exceptional it is relative to the conditional knowledge base) and read each case as normally as possible. phi |~ psi holds if rank(phi&psi) < rank(phi&not psi). Known flaw, called drowning: in the review's example the ranks of 'l & f' and 'l & not f' are equal (both 1), so a property is not inherited by an exceptional subclass. Lehmann (1995) lexicographic closure repairs this by comparing severity of violations.
numbers: Example ranks: l=1, c=0, r=0, f=0, l&f=1, l&not f=1. Ranks are natural numbers from an iterated material-counterpart test.
limits: Rational closure is one canonical answer, not the only one, and drowning shows it can be too cautious.
agent_relevance: A rank of exceptionality is a codeable way to order lessons: the more exceptional the case, the more specific the lesson it needs. Gives a non-LLM rule for which lesson wins.

source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Non-monotonic Logic, specificity and non-monotonic inheritance
finding: Specificity principle: more specific information overrides more generic (a baby bat does not fly although bats have default links to flying). Reiter's default logic has no priority among defaults; Poole (1985) added specificity; Horty (2007) orders defaults by a strict partial order. Non-monotonic inheritance networks (is-a links with exceptions) define extensions of networks, with competing sceptical and credulous readings.
numbers: Qualitative. Example: Stellaluna the baby bat.
limits: Different path-based semantics give different answers on the same network; no single winner.
agent_relevance: For lessons with exceptions, a code-checked rule 'narrower scope beats wider scope' resolves most conflicts without asking a model.

source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Non-monotonic Logic, autoepistemic logic and answer sets
finding: Moore's autoepistemic logic: a default means 'unless I know otherwise'. Extensions are stable expansions, closed under: if A is in E then Box A is in E; if A is not in E then not-Box A is in E. Its belief operator is indexical, so its meaning changes with the theory it sits in. Gelfond and Lifschitz (1988) showed that stable-model semantics of logic programs with negation as failure is equivalent to an autoepistemic translation; this is the base of answer set programming.
numbers: Translation: 'phi1,...,phin, not psi' maps to 'phi1 & ... & phin & not-B psi implies phi'.
limits: Several semantics exist (S5-style, bimodal Lin-Shoham); links to default logic hold for restricted fragments.
agent_relevance: Negation as failure in a rule engine is the closest executable form of 'conclude unless known otherwise'. The Revise trigger can be implemented as such a rule over a fact table.

source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Defeasible Reasoning (Koons), Pollock's defeaters and gaps in default logic
finding: Pollock separates two defeaters: rebutting (a reason for the opposite conclusion) and undercutting (a reason to doubt the link between premises and conclusion in this case). Reiter-style default logic cannot represent undercutting defeaters and has no built-in specificity. A conclusion is warranted if supported by an ultimately undefeated argument. Default logic also fails on disjunctive facts: Smith is Amish or Quaker, both normally pacifists, does not yield 'pacifist'.
numbers: Qualitative; cites Pollock 1967 to 2010 and Horty 2007 for priorities and higher-order defaults.
limits: Review claims, not new data.
agent_relevance: Maps onto Revise: a failed test rebuts; a signal that the test itself is unreliable (flaky check, bad held-out set) undercuts. The retraction log needs both labels.

source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: The Frame Problem (inertia default and the Yale shooting problem)
finding: The technical frame problem is formalising the common-sense law of inertia: nothing changes unless there is evidence. Classical logic cannot, because it is monotonic and each new exception would need a new axiom. Hanks and McDermott (1987) Yale shooting problem showed naive non-monotonic formalisms give an unintended answer. The review says solutions now exist and the technical problem is 'more-or-less solved'.
numbers: Scenario: Fred, gun loaded at 1, wait, shoot at 3. Two minimal-change models: intended (Fred dies) and spurious (gun unloads by itself, Fred lives).
limits: The 'solved' verdict is for the logic-based AI case; concurrency, nondeterminism and ramifications were hard.
agent_relevance: Warning: minimising change naively can pick the wrong story. When a state persists by default, the model must not choose where an unexplained change happened; record a cause.

source: Wikipedia: Yale shooting problem (secondary)
finding: Proposed by Steve Hanks and Drew McDermott at Yale in a 1985 paper (AAAI Classic Paper award 2005; AIJ version 1987, 'Nonmonotonic logic and temporal projection'). Fixes: predicate completion (effect as if-and-only-if), Sandewall's occlusion (minimise permissions to change rather than changes), Reiter's situation calculus, fluent calculus, action languages.
numbers: Time points 0 to 3, fluents alive and loaded.
limits: Encyclopedia summary, not the primary paper.
agent_relevance: The occlusion idea (minimise permissions to change, not changes) is a usable design: Revise may change only what the failing output names.

source: Wikipedia: Default logic (secondary), complexity and normal defaults
finding: Propositional default logic: existence of an extension is Sigma2P-complete; skeptical entailment Pi2P-complete; credulous entailment Sigma2P-complete; extension checking Delta2P[log]-complete. A default is normal if its justification equals its conclusion; normal theories always have an extension. The Nixon theory has two extensions.
numbers: Complexity classes as listed; page cites Gottlob (1992) and Liberatore and Schaerf (1998) but does not tie each result to a paper.
limits: Secondary. Attribution of each result not verified. Propositional case only.
agent_relevance: Full default reasoning is intractable beyond small theories, so keep the default set small and normal and let code check it.

source: Wikipedia: Answer set programming (secondary)
finding: ASP targets hard (mostly NP-hard) search problems under stable-model semantics, with 'not' as default negation. Example: choice rule 1{p,q,r}2 with rule 's :- not p' gives six stable models. The term answer set programming appeared in 1999 (Marek and Truszczynski; Niemela). Solvers: smodels, clasp, DLV, gringo.
numbers: Six stable models: {p,q}, {p}, {p,r}, {q,s}, {r,s}, {q,r,s}.
limits: Page does not name Gelfond and Lifschitz or give complexity of the reasoning tasks.
agent_relevance: A ready-made terminating tool (clasp) can run default rules with exceptions for our agent; the model only translates text into facts.

source: Gelfond and Lifschitz stable models, as presented in Ren et al. (2025)
finding: The semantics of an ASP program is given by the Gelfond-Lifschitz transformation: guess a set S, delete rules blocked by S, delete 'not' from the rest, and check S is the least model. Answer sets are stable models. ASP is presented as the practical home of default reasoning (Reiter 1980) with links to belief revision.
numbers: Describes the three ASPBench tasks: answer set entailment (ASE), verification (ASV), computation (ASC).
limits: The original Gelfond and Lifschitz PDF text was garbled on extraction, so only this presentation of it is cited.
agent_relevance: Same guess-and-check shape as Reiter extensions: a program can check a proposed belief set cheaply, which suits 'code selects' (G5).

source: Ren, Xiao, Qi, Geng, Xue (2025) Can LLMs solve ASP problems? ASPBench
finding: Benchmark of three ASP tasks with 14 LLMs (including deepseek-r1, o4-mini, gemini-2.5-flash-thinking, o3-mini). A steep cliff with task complexity: average F1 68.8% on entailment (ASE) and 64.7% on verification (ASV), but exact match on computing answer sets (ASC) only 23.2% on synthetic programs and 8.6% on 47 real-world programs. Reasoning models help a lot.
numbers: ASE peak 98.2% (o3-mini, symbolic input); ASV peak 87.2% (deepseek-r1). ASC EM: deepseek-r1 55.7% vs deepseek-v3 20.7%; qwen3-14b 9.2% vs qwen2.5-14b 1.4%. Text slightly better for ASE (70.4 vs 67.2 F1); symbolic slightly better for ASC (24.0 vs 22.4 EM). Real programs: ASV F1 64.7 to 57.6. ASC EM falls over 20 points with unstratified cycles. Predicted 'unknown' 47.2% vs 26.6% true.
limits: Single study on symbolic programs, not natural-language defaults. Risk-averse bias toward 'unknown'. Completeness blind spot: correct answer sets and ones missing one fact misjudged at similar rates (41% vs 39%).
agent_relevance: LLMs should not compute stable models or extensions themselves. Let code do it and give the model only the job of writing facts. The pull toward 'unknown' is a reminder that models over-doubt, which is the G1 risk.

source: Yang, Ishay, Lee (2023) Coupling LLMs with logic programming for robust and general reasoning from text
finding: GPT-3 is used as a few-shot semantic parser into facts; an answer set program with reusable knowledge modules (including the commonsense law of inertia in event calculus, a default rule) does the reasoning. State of the art on bAbI, StepGame, CLUTRR and gSCAN, and solves robot planning that the LLM alone fails.
numbers: bAbI: text-davinci-003 few-shot 80.34%, with chain of thought 86.18%, with ASP 99.99% average over 20 tasks. Pick&Place planning: GPT-3 alone 0% whole-plan accuracy but 100% fact-extraction accuracy; planning solved with ASP. StepGame: GPT-3 baselines run on only the first 100 test samples vs 1,000 for the ASP method.
limits: Knowledge modules are hand-written. Baselines evaluated on smaller samples because of cost. Not a test of exception handling in free text.
agent_relevance: Direct support for the split: the model translates, code reasons with defaults. Matches section 1 of the schema (program decides, model fills a slot).

source: Tachmazidis, Batsakis, Antoniou (2024) Benchmarking defeasible reasoning with LLMs
finding: Turns the defeasible-logic test suite of Maher et al. (2001) into text: 'typically' marks defeasible rules, and imaginary species ('Arkon') block world knowledge, following Ford and Billington (2000). GPT-4o with 'think step by step' on 8 theories in 4 settings (conclusion negated or not; statements in random or sequential order).
numbers: Of 32 theory-setting cells, 25 were correct and 7 wrong (about 78%). Theory levels-(5) (conflicting rules, no priorities) was wrong in all 4 settings; levels(5) wrong twice; dag(3,2) once. Circle theories correctly give no conclusion. One run invented a fact ('A0000002 is typically an Arkon'). Statement order changed the outcome in some theories.
quote: Preliminary experiments indicated encouraging results for monotonic reasoning as well as certain challenges in the context of non-monotonic rule-based reasoning
limits: Tiny: 8 theories, one model, one run per cell, no intervals. Authors call it preliminary.
agent_relevance: The failure is where rules conflict with no priority: exactly where the schema needs a code-side tie-break. Order effects mean checks should be run on shuffled inputs.

source: Kirkpatrick and Sterken (2025) Generics and default reasoning in LLMs
finding: 28 LLMs on 20 defeasible inference patterns with generics (Birds fly), 20 instances per pattern; zero-shot, few-shot, zero-shot chain of thought; temperature 0 and 1. Several frontier models exceed 90% on 15 uncontroversial patterns. Chain of thought often hurts.
numbers: Zero-shot accuracy: Claude 3 Opus 96.51, Claude 3.5 Sonnet 96.01, GPT-4 (0613) 93.52, GPT-4 Turbo 92.69, Gemma 2 9B 92.69, GPT-4o (2024-08) 89.03; lowest Code Llama 34B 6.48. CoT mean change -11.14 points (SD 15.74) among models above 75% zero-shot. CoT deltas: Llama 2 70B -41.52, Llama 2 13B -41.03, Yi 34B -33.22, GPT-4 (0613) -12.62, Gemini 1.5 Flash -18.77, Claude 3.5 Sonnet -0.33. Few-shot gains modest for most.
quote: chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting often leads to serious performance degradation
limits: Yes/no single-token scoring; one-step inferences only. Authors give two unseparated explanations for the CoT loss: overthinking, or conceptual gaps. Error analysis on only 3 models.
agent_relevance: Strong match to G1 and G11: more deliberation on a default inference degrades it. For default-style questions, answer briefly and leave doubt to a signal.

source: Kirkpatrick and Sterken (2025): do LLMs treat generics as universals?
finding: Three matched versions of 8 patterns: defeasible question with generics (base); deductive question with generics (v; the correct answer is 'does not follow'); deductive question with universals (va). Models often said 'follows deductively' to a generic premise, treating 'Cats are cute' like 'All cats are cute'. CoT error types: generic read as universal; defeasible-deductive confusion; over-statistical; step-consistent but bad conclusion.
numbers: Mean accuracy over 28 models, base / v / va: DMP 80.50 / 25.06 / 74.77; DMT 80.30 / 34.48 / 69.30; DI 72.99 / 30.06 / 65.42; FI 75.77 / 31.23 / 67.67; DDMP 86.96 / 90.20 / 6.98. Correlation base vs v across models: DMP -0.68, DI -0.84, DDMP +0.90 (p<.01).
limits: Which variant is scored as correct for v follows the paper's description; table headers were garbled in extraction. Temperature 0.
agent_relevance: Models over-apply defaults as certainties. Store a lesson as 'normally X, unless Y' with its exception list, not as a flat rule the model will read as universal.

source: Kirkpatrick and Sterken (2025): irrelevance, disabled defaults, premise order
finding: Five irrelevance patterns: an exceptional individual should not affect others; an irrelevant fact or default should not block an inference; a possibly exceptional other individual should not disable the default. Top models passed zero-shot; weaker ones were at or below chance until few-shot. GPT-4o (2024-05-13) was at chance on basic default reasoning and on disabled default, improving in few-shot. Premise order mattered: specific-first helped several models zero-shot, reversed in few-shot, and GPT-4 Turbo (1106) fell below chance with specific-first on modus tollens.
numbers: Example: heavy blocks are on the table, A and B are heavy, A is not on the table, so infer B is on the table. Fact irrelevance: Claude 3 Haiku and GPT-3.5 (1106) rose from 75% to 100% in few-shot.
limits: Per-pattern, per-model values are in appendix figures; only some were read. Mixed temperature effects.
agent_relevance: A failure on case A must not retract the lesson for case B. Test this with a mutated-input check (G3).

source: Kazemi et al. (2023) BoardgameQA: reasoning with contradictory information
finding: A defeasible theory is facts, rules and pairwise rule priorities (newer source beats older; 'penguins do not fly' beats 'birds fly'). Type1 conflicts can be dodged if the conflicting rule's body cannot be proved; Type2 need one body element shown false. Models: BERT-large and T5-XXL fine-tuned, PaLM 62B prompt-tuned, PaLM 540B few-shot with chain of thought.
numbers: Conflict probability 0.0, 0.2, 0.5, 0.8 (NoConflict to HighConflict). All models degrade steadily with more conflict; BERT drops to near random at Medium and High. Few-shot PaLM is weak at the right conflict resolution (Conflict F1); tuned models do much better. Type1 easier than Type2. Exact accuracies are only in figures, so not recorded here.
quote: LMs perform poorly when reasoning with conflicting sources, especially in the few-shot setting
limits: Could not read figure values from the PDF text. Synthetic board-game rules with missing knowledge to be supplied by the model. PaLM-era models.
agent_relevance: Priorities between rules must be given or computed by code, not left to a few-shot model. Conflicts with no explicit priority are the hard case.

source: Parmar et al. (2024) LogicBench: 25 reasoning patterns including non-monotonic
finding: The non-monotonic part follows Lifschitz's 1989 benchmark problems: basic default, default with irrelevant information (DRI), several defaults (DRS), disabled default (DRD), open domain (DRO), unknown expectations (RE1, RE2), priorities (RAP). Five models with chain of thought, zero-shot: GPT-4, ChatGPT, Gemini-Pro, Llama-2-7B, Mistral-7B. Models do better on non-monotonic and first-order patterns than on propositional ones, and worse when there are several defaults.
numbers: NM block averages, yes-label / no-label accuracy (column mapping is my reading of a garbled table): Llama-2 57.78 / 43.74; Mistral 71.00 / 67.49; Gemini 67.78 / 69.71; ChatGPT 61.47 / 65.46; GPT-4 74.43 / 84.75. Propositional yes-label: ChatGPT 48.04, GPT-4 63.98. Human check on 50 instances with 3 annotators: below ceiling, and NM multiple-choice stays hard for both humans and LLMs.
limits: Small human subset. Table layout garbled so column mapping is inferred. Authors speculate that models saw non-monotonic phrasing ('normally birds fly') in training text.
agent_relevance: The weak spot is several defaults at once (DRS). Keep each lesson's exception list short and resolve conflicts in code.

source: Rudinger et al. (2020) Thinking like a skeptic: Defeasible NLI (delta-NLI)
finding: Dataset: given premise and hypothesis, an update sentence is a strengthener or weakener. Three sources: SNLI, ATOMIC, SOCIAL-CHEM-101. Classifying is easy for RoBERTa-base; generating weakeners and strengtheners is much harder.
numbers: Test accuracy, RoBERTa vs human: delta-SNLI 81.6 vs 83.6; delta-ATOMIC 78.3 vs 78.2; delta-SOCIAL 86.2 vs 87.6; majority about 50. Update-only baseline 65.1, 65.2, 71.6, which is 15 to 20 points above majority (annotation artifacts) and 13 to 15 below full input. Example sizes: SNLI train 19,518 rows; ATOMIC test 2,327.
quote: an inference (X is a bird, therefore X flies) may be weakened or overturned in light of new evidence (X is a penguin)
limits: Pre-LLM (RoBERTa, GPT-2). Crowd-written updates carry artifacts. Generation judged by small human samples.
agent_relevance: Models can tell which way new evidence pushes a claim but find it hard to invent such evidence. Supports G2: let code supply the failing output, let the model judge direction.

source: Allaway et al. (2023) Penguins don't fly: generics through instantiations and exceptions
finding: A framework generates exemplars for generics: instantiations (cases where the generic holds) and exceptions. It produced 12,562 instantiations and 6,297 exceptions for 650 generics, beating a GPT-3 few-shot baseline by 12.8 precision points on average. Exceptions are harder: 71% of generated instantiations are true versus 40% of exceptions; the validity discriminator accepts 77% versus 50%. NLI labels cannot separate true-but-not-entailed cases from unknown ones.
numbers: 650 generics (from a 768-generic subset above probability 0.5); about 19k exemplars total; the baseline for exceptions was close to random.
limits: Human referents excluded; pre-GPT-4 models; crowd-worker evaluation.
agent_relevance: Listing exceptions is hard even for a model, so collect them from observed failures, not by asking the model to imagine them.

source: Comparison of the four formal families (assembled from McCarthy 1980/1986, SEP, Koons)
finding: Four families give 'retract on new evidence': circumscription (minimise abnormal things), Reiter default logic (fixed-point extensions with justifications), autoepistemic logic and stable models ('unless known otherwise'), and KLM preferential models with rational closure (order models by normality). They agree on easy penguin cases and differ on conflicting defaults with no priority, floating conclusions and disjunctive facts.
numbers: None quantitative. Propositional versions sit at the second level of the polynomial hierarchy (Sigma2P / Pi2P).
limits: Equivalences hold only on fragments. This angle did not test which family best matches human behaviour; left to other angles.
agent_relevance: Pick the simplest executable form: negation as failure over a short list of normal defaults with specificity priorities, run by code. Richer semantics add cost with no evidence of gain for us.
